A strikingly clean design was offered by Parrish et al. (2015), who demonstrated

     the decoy effect in a perceptual discrimination task with rhesus macaques. In the present study,

     we sought to extend their paradigm to human participants to determine whether the same effect

     would emerge.

targets.authors: Parrish, A. E., Evans, T. A., & Beran, M. J.
targets.title: Rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) exhibit the decoy effect in a perceptual discrimination task.
targets.evidence_quote:
A strikingly clean design was offered by Parrish et al. (2015), who demonstrated

     the decoy effect in a perceptual discrimination task with rhesus macaques. In the present study,

     we sought to extend their paradigm to human participants to determine whether the same effect

     would emerge.
targets.outcome_quote:
The present study aimed to determine whether the decoy effect would emerge in a human

     perceptual discrimination task. Contrary to our predictions and to findings in rhesus macaques

     (Parrish et al., 2015), we found no reliable evidence of a decoy effect.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly conclude that their human test found no reliable decoy effect, contrary to the macaque finding. This is the central effect and overall verdict; exploratory orientation and difficulty effects do not change it.

reasoning: New human participants retest the published macaque decoy finding. The methods identify Experiment 2 of Parrish et al. (2015). Other perceptual and value-based studies provide background or mechanistic context and are not independently retested targets. The paper reports completed data collection and results.
